attraction_name_en: Longjing Tea Plantation / Dragon Well Tea Village
address_cn: 浙江省杭州市西湖区龙井村
hook: The birthplace of China's most celebrated green tea — walk through 1,200 years of tea history, pick leaves alongside farmers, watch them hand-fry in a red-hot wok, and taste the result while sitting in the home of the family who grew it.
honest_description: Longjing Tea Plantation covers the broader tea-growing region southwest of West Lake, encompassing several villages including Longjing Village, Meijiawu, and surrounding hillside plantations. It's a genuinely beautiful area — rolling hills blanketed in perfectly manicured rows of tea bushes, clean air, and a slower pace of life that feels miles from the city. The main experience is wandering through the plantations, visiting farmhouses for tea tasting, and optionally participating in tea picking or watching the traditional hand-frying process. However, virtually every interaction with locals ends in a tea sales pitch, and prices are steep (premium Longjing runs ¥1600+ per jin/500g). The area is free to enter and open all day, with no formal structure — you set your own pace. Spring (March-April) is magical during the harvest, but also the most crowded. In summer it's searingly hot with aggressive mosquitoes. The villages are a bit spread out and public transport is limited, so plan your logistics. Best for tea enthusiasts, photographers, and anyone wanting a half-day escape from West Lake's crowds into the peaceful green hills.

foreigner_top_questions.question: Can I actually pick tea leaves and see how Longjing tea is made?
foreigner_top_questions.answer: Yes — during the spring harvest season (late March to early May), many farms offer tea-picking experiences where you carry a bamboo basket and pluck leaves alongside workers. Afterward, you can watch the hand-frying (炒茶) process in a hot wok. Outside spring, picking isn't available but you can still watch demonstrations and do tastings at farmhouses. Guided tours through Klook or Trip.com are the easiest way to arrange this as a foreigner. Our concierge team can also match you with a vetted English-speaking guide who knows the tea villages well — they'll handle transport, translate during tea tastings, and make sure you don't overpay.

foreigner_top_questions.question: How much should Longjing tea cost, and how do I avoid getting ripped off?
foreigner_top_questions.answer: Genuine West Lake Longjing is expensive everywhere. Top-grade Mingqian (pre-Qingming) tea runs ¥800-1600+ per 500g even from farmers. Later harvests are ¥200-500. Tourist prices are typically 2x the real price — bargain aggressively (start at half). Buy small quantities (50-100g) as souvenirs. For fixed, fair pricing, visit the China National Tea Museum shop nearby or buy from the village committee (村委会). A Google review notes ¥1600/500g for top-grade, which is in the expected range.

experience_format_note: Open, free-roaming experience with no formal entry, tickets, or set route. Multiple villages and tea farms spread across hilly terrain southwest of West Lake. You walk at your own pace through the plantations and village lanes, stopping at farmhouses for tea tasting. No English signage or guides unless you arrange one privately.
vibe: Serene, green, and fragrant — a living landscape where centuries-old tea traditions continue in the shadow of a modern city, and every conversation eventually leads to a cup of tea.

time_needed.quick_visit: 1-2 hours (bus to Longjing Village, walk through main tea fields, one tea tasting)
time_needed.recommended: 3-4 hours (explore tea terraces, tea tasting, visit Eighteen Imperial Tea Trees, walk to Nine Creeks trail)
time_needed.deep_dive: Full day (combine Longjing Village, Meijiawu Tea Village, China National Tea Museum, Nine Creeks hike, and Hupao Spring)

best_time.best_time_of_day: Early morning (7-9 AM) when tea farmers are actively picking, the light is golden on the fields, and tourist crowds haven't arrived yet.
best_time.worst_time: Midday in July-August — temperatures exceed 40°C with virtually no shade on the exposed hillside paths. Weekends during spring harvest (March-April) draw huge domestic crowds.
best_time.seasonal_notes: Spring (March-May) is the absolute peak: tea picking is underway, the fields are luminous green, and you can taste the freshest possible Longjing. The prized Mingqian tea is picked before Qingming Festival (early April). Summer is green but brutally hot. Autumn (September-November) has comfortable weather and osmanthus fragrance mixing with tea scent. Winter is quiet and dormant — peaceful but less scenic.
best_time.pro_tip: Visit in mid-March on a weekday to catch the very first spring harvest (the earliest, most prized 'first flush' leaves). The village is busy but not packed, and farmers are in the best mood after a good crop.

getting_in.opening_hours: Open all day, year-round. No gates or closing times. Individual farmhouses keep their own hours but most welcome visitors from sunrise to evening.
getting_in.price_rmb: Free (village access). Old Longjing Imperial Tea Garden (老龙井御茶园) is ¥10.

price_breakdown.item: Longjing Village and tea fields access
price_breakdown.highlight: Walk freely through all public tea fields and village paths

price_breakdown.item: Old Longjing Imperial Tea Garden (老龙井御茶园)
price_breakdown.highlight: Includes the Eighteen Imperial Tea Trees, Longquan spring, and Song Dynasty temple ruins
You'll be offered free cups but expected to purchase tea — ¥50-500+ depending on grade and quantity

getting_in.booking_required: No — just show up. For organized tea-picking experiences or English-speaking guided tours, book in advance through Klook or Trip.com.
getting_in.booking_method: Walk-in for self-guided visits. Klook, Trip.com, or GetYourGuide for guided experiences with transport.
getting_in.passport_accepted: N/A — no formal ticketing. The Imperial Tea Garden accepts cash at the gate.
getting_in.what_to_bring: Comfortable walking shoes. Mosquito repellent (critical May-October). Water bottle. Cash for tea purchases. Sunscreen and hat in summer. Translation app if you don't speak Mandarin.
getting_in.queue_situation: No queues in the tea fields. Bus 27 can be crowded during spring weekends. Farmhouse tea tastings have no wait.
getting_in.language_barrier_rating: chinese-only — No English signage anywhere. Villagers speak Mandarin and/or local Hangzhou dialect. A few tour operators offer English guides. Translation app essential for solo foreign visitors.

highlights.name: Tea Terraces and Plantation Walks
highlights.description: Thousands of acres of precisely manicured tea bushes blanketing the hillsides in rows that follow the terrain's contours. In spring, straw-hatted workers move through the rows hand-picking leaves. The visual effect — endless rolling green — is genuinely stunning.
highlights.foreigner_note: Multiple Google reviewers describe this as 'zen,' 'serene,' and 'like walking through a painting.' Even non-tea-drinkers are moved by the landscape beauty.
highlights.tip: Walk uphill away from the main road to find less-visited terraces. The tea bushes on higher ground produce better tea and offer better views.

highlights.name: Eighteen Imperial Tea Trees (十八棵御茶)
highlights.description: The legendary tea bushes personally designated by Emperor Qianlong during his visit in the Qing Dynasty. According to legend, tea from these specific bushes cured his mother's illness, and he granted them 'imperial' status. Located in the Old Longjing Imperial Tea Garden.
highlights.foreigner_note: The trees themselves are small and fenced off, but the story is compelling — and understanding it adds context to why Longjing tea is so revered in Chinese culture.
highlights.tip: The ¥10 entry to the garden is worth it — the grounds also include the ancient Dragon Well spring and atmospheric Song Dynasty temple ruins.

highlights.name: Farmhouse Tea Tasting Experience
highlights.description: Local families invite visitors into their homes to sit around a tea table while they brew multiple grades of Longjing tea, explaining the differences. You learn to distinguish Mingqian from Yuqian, compare leaf shapes, and observe how water temperature affects flavor.
highlights.foreigner_note: This is the real deal — you're tasting tea in the home of the person who grew it, not in a tourist center. Several Google reviewers call it a highlight of their Hangzhou trip despite the sales pressure.
highlights.tip: Ask to see different grades side-by-side. The visual and taste differences between ¥200 and ¥800 tea are dramatic and educational. Buy a small packet of mid-grade tea — it's perfectly good and more reasonably priced.

highlights.name: Meijiawu Tea Village (梅家坞)
highlights.description: A separate village 13km west of West Lake with 600+ years of tea history, visited by Queen Elizabeth and Premier Zhou Enlai. More spread out and rural than Longjing Village, with dozens of tea houses and restaurants serving tea-infused cuisine (Longjing shrimp is the signature dish).
highlights.foreigner_note: Described as 'the most real and original place where Dragon Well tea is produced' — less touristy than Longjing Village itself. Several foreign visitors specifically recommend it.
highlights.tip: Take bus 28 or a taxi (¥35-45 from central Hangzhou). Come for lunch — the tea-infused local cuisine here is excellent and not overpriced.

what_visitors_miss.what: China National Tea Museum (中国茶叶博物馆)
what_visitors_miss.why: Free, well-curated museum covering the full history and culture of Chinese tea. Most visitors go straight to the villages and skip this — but visiting the museum first gives you the knowledge to appreciate the tea tasting much more, and their tea shop has fair, fixed pricing.

Longjing tea's flat leaf shape comes from being hand-pressed in a 240-300°C wok — a UNESCO-recognized skill. Skilled workers can only produce about 1kg of finished tea per day. Most tourists just taste the end product without seeing this incredible process. Ask at farmhouses during spring season.

The ride from the tea villages back to West Lake is mostly downhill through beautiful scenery. Shared bikes (Mobike, Hellobike) are cheap and available — multiple reviewers recommend this as a highlight. Much more enjoyable than waiting for an infrequent bus.

strategy.smart_route: Take bus 27 from the north shore of West Lake to Longjing Tea Village stop (¥2, 25 min) → walk through the main tea fields → visit Old Longjing Imperial Tea Garden (¥10) to see the Eighteen Imperial Tea Trees → accept a farmhouse tea tasting → walk or take a Didi to Meijiawu for lunch → visit the China National Tea Museum (free) on the way back → bike or bus back to West Lake.
strategy.what_to_skip: Skip the overpriced tea shops right at the bus stop — walk further in for better prices and more authentic experiences. Skip Longjing Village on weekends during March-April peak season — go to the quieter Meijiawu instead.
strategy.pro_tips: Download a translation app before visiting — it makes tea tasting and bargaining infinitely easier. Bring a refillable water bottle — locals insist the best Longjing must be brewed with local spring water, and several springs are accessible. For the best souvenir, buy 50-100g of mid-grade Yuqian tea — it's half the price of Mingqian and still excellent.

heads_up.warning: Every interaction eventually becomes a tea sales pitch
heads_up.advice: This is the culture here — hospitality and commerce are intertwined. Enjoy the tea tasting, learn something, and either buy a small amount or politely decline. Don't let the commercial aspect ruin what's genuinely a beautiful experience. Set a budget before you start.

heads_up.warning: Tea prices are not standardized and tourists get overcharged
heads_up.advice: Bargaining is expected and necessary — multiple Chinese reviewers confirm you should negotiate to 50-60% of the asking price. If a farmer quotes ¥800 for a small packet, counter with ¥400. Walk away if they won't budge — the next house will. If you want a second opinion mid-negotiation, send us a photo of the tea and the asking price — our team can tell you instantly whether it's fair.

heads_up.warning: The area is spread out with limited transport between villages
heads_up.advice: Longjing Village and Meijiawu are not within walking distance of each other. Plan your transport: bus 27 serves Longjing Village; bus 28 serves Meijiawu. Didi works but signal can be patchy in the hills. A guided tour solves all transport headaches. We can also arrange a private car for a half-day tea village tour — the driver waits while you explore each stop, which makes covering both villages stress-free.

heads_up.warning: Noisy vehicles on village roads can disrupt the peace
heads_up.advice: Tour buses and cars with honking horns share the narrow village roads. Walk the smaller footpaths between tea rows rather than along the main road for a quieter experience.

foreigners_watch_out: No English signage or English speakers anywhere in the villages. A translation app is essential for meaningful interaction. Even the Google Maps labeling in this area can be inconsistent. If you're struggling with communication at any point, message our concierge team — we can translate via chat, call a farmer on your behalf, or send you voice notes in Mandarin to play for the person you're talking to.

Hotel drivers may offer to 'take you to the tea village' — this is common and usually involves them taking you to a specific farmhouse where they get a commission, resulting in higher prices for you. Take the bus or Didi independently instead.
Payment is cash or WeChat/Alipay only. No foreign credit cards are accepted at farmhouses, small restaurants, or the Imperial Tea Garden. Bring Chinese cash.

The tea-picking experience requires bare hands on delicate plants — some farms may be hesitant to let clumsy visitors pick from their best bushes. Be gentle and follow instructions, or book a tourist-oriented picking experience through a tour company.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: Can't find transport back to the city center
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: Head to the main Longjing Village bus stop for bus 27, which runs frequently. If no bus, try Didi — walk to the village center for better phone signal.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: Rent a shared bike (Mobike, Hellobike) and ride downhill back to West Lake — takes about 20-25 minutes and is actually a great experience. Multiple reviewers recommend this.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: Bought expensive tea and not sure if it's genuine
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: If you purchased from a farmhouse in the designated West Lake Longjing growing area, it's almost certainly genuine — the concern is more about overpaying than fake tea. Real Longjing leaves are flat, smooth, and uniformly green.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: For guaranteed quality with receipts, buy from the China National Tea Museum shop or a licensed vendor in Longjing Village. These have fixed prices and quality certification.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: Weather turns rainy during your visit
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: Rain actually enhances the atmosphere — misty tea terraces are incredibly photogenic and the air smells amazing. Farmers continue working in light rain. Bring a rain jacket or compact umbrella.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: Head to the China National Tea Museum (indoor, free) or find a covered farmhouse tea room to wait it out with a pot of tea. Rainy-day tea tasting is actually very atmospheric. If you get caught without rain gear, message us — we can have an umbrella or poncho delivered to the nearest village bus stop.

preparation.what_to_wear: Comfortable walking shoes with good grip — paths can be slippery, especially on damp tea terraces. Long sleeves and pants help against mosquitoes and sun. Layers in spring and autumn — it can be cool in the hills in the morning.
preparation.what_to_bring: Mosquito repellent (essential in warmer months). Water bottle. Cash (¥200-500 depending on how much tea you plan to buy). Phone with translation app and Didi installed. Sunscreen and hat. A small bag to carry tea purchases.
preparation.what_not_to_bring: Heavy luggage — this is a walking experience on hilly terrain. Expectations of air conditioning or Western food.

physical_accessibility.physical_details: Main village roads are paved and relatively flat. Tea terraces involve hilly terrain with narrow paths and some uneven surfaces. The walk from bus stop to tea fields is about 1-2km. Total walking for a typical visit is 3-6km with moderate elevation changes.
physical_accessibility.age_notes: Suitable for moderately fit visitors of all ages on main paths. The hillside terraces may challenge elderly visitors or those with mobility issues. No wheelchair access on tea field paths.
physical_accessibility.health_warnings: Extreme heat in summer (regularly 40°C) with no shade on exposed hillsides — heat stroke risk is real. Mosquitoes carry diseases — use repellent. The hilly terrain means some cardiovascular effort.

concierge_opportunities.action: Book a guided Longjing tea experience with transport
concierge_opportunities.value_to_user: Solves the transport puzzle, provides an English-speaking guide who explains tea culture and history, includes organized tea picking (in season) and tasting, and prevents getting overcharged on tea purchases. Usually ¥200-400 per person.

concierge_opportunities.action: Book a half-day West Lake + Tea Village combo tour
concierge_opportunities.value_to_user: Combines the tea plantation visit with West Lake highlights in a single guided half-day — efficient use of time and eliminates transport logistics.

pair_with.suggestion: China National Tea Museum (中国茶叶博物馆)
pair_with.why: Free museum dedicated to Chinese tea history and culture — provides the knowledge foundation that makes the tea village tasting much richer. Their gift shop sells authenticated tea at fair prices.

pair_with.suggestion: Nine Creeks and Eighteen Gullies (九溪十八涧)
pair_with.why: One of Hangzhou's most peaceful nature walks — a creek-side trail through bamboo forests that connects to the tea plantation area. Perfect cool-down after a hot hillside walk.
The tea villages are just 20-30 minutes from West Lake's south shore. A morning at the tea plantation followed by an afternoon lakeside walk makes an ideal full day.
pair_with.travel_time: 20 minutes by bus 27 or 25 minutes by bike (downhill)

cultural_context: Longjing tea has been grown in these specific hills for over 1,200 years, making this one of the world's oldest continuously cultivated tea regions. The tea's fame skyrocketed when Qing Dynasty Emperor Qianlong visited, declared it the finest tea in China, and granted 'imperial' status to eighteen specific bushes — still alive today. West Lake Longjing is a protected geographical indication: only tea from these designated areas can legally carry the name, similar to Champagne. The traditional hand-frying technique (using bare hands on a 300°C wok) was recognized as national intangible cultural heritage in 2008. For Chinese visitors, drinking fresh Longjing at its source is a culturally loaded experience — it connects them to 1,200 years of literati, emperors, and Buddhist monks who sat in these same hills and drank the same tea.

photo_spots.location: Hillside tea rows above Longjing Village
photo_spots.tip: Walk uphill from the village until you can see rows stretching in multiple directions. Early morning light (7-8 AM) creates the best contrast between the bright green leaves and misty hills behind.
photo_spots.why: The vanishing-point perspective of perfectly aligned tea rows against a mountain backdrop is the classic Longjing image.

photo_spots.tip: March-April mornings — look for workers in traditional straw hats and blue clothing among the bushes. Ask permission before photographing closely. A telephoto lens helps capture candid moments without intruding.
photo_spots.why: Human figures in the vast green landscape add scale and cultural context — these images tell a story that empty fields cannot.

photo_spots.location: Eighteen Imperial Tea Trees (十八棵御茶)
photo_spots.tip: The trees are small and fenced — get low and shoot upward to include the hillside behind. A sign with the history makes a good establishing shot.
photo_spots.why: The historical significance makes this a 'proof of visit' shot — the trees themselves are modest, but the story is extraordinary.

photo_spots.location: Tea terraces with village houses below
photo_spots.tip: Find a high vantage point where white-walled, dark-roofed village houses sit among the green tea rows. Overcast or misty days create an ethereal Chinese painting aesthetic.
photo_spots.why: The contrast between the geometric tea rows and organic architecture captures the essence of this centuries-old landscape.

card_hook: Twelve hundred years of tea, straight from the hillside to your cup.
